A put option is a financial derivative that gives the holder the right, but not the obligation, to sell an underlying asset at a specified price (called the strike price) by a specific date (the expiration date). The details of a put option typically include:

1. Strike Price: This is the price at which the seller of the put option is required to buy the underlying asset from the buyer of the put.

2. Expiration Date: This is the date on which the put option expires and its value becomes invalid.

3. Premium: This is the cost of purchasing the put option. It is paid to the seller of the put by the buyer and represents the compensation for giving up the right to buy the underlying asset at the strike price.

4. Underlying Asset: This is the stock or other financial instrument over which the put option is being exercised. 

5. Exercise Price: This is the price at which the put option can be exercised, i.e., the buyer can exercise the option to sell the underlying asset.

6. Intrinsic Value: This is the difference between the strike price and the market price of the underlying asset. If the market price is higher than the strike price, the intrinsic value is zero; if it is lower, the intrinsic value is positive and equals the difference between the two prices.

7. Time Value: This is the additional value of the put option beyond its intrinsic value, representing the possibility of the underlying asset's price moving in favor of the buyer in the future.

8. Type of Put Option: There are two types of put options - American-style and European-style. American-style put options can be exercised at any time before the expiration date, while European-style put options can only be exercised on the expiration date. 

9. Implied Volatility: This is a measure of the expected volatility of the price of the underlying asset over the life of the option. The higher the implied volatility, the more expensive the put option will be.
